utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-08-91-T. The Prosecutor versus Mico Stanisic and Stojan Zupljanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Good morning to everyone. May we begin by taking the appearances, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Joanna Korner, Belinda Pidwell, Crispian Smith, for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Slobodan Zecevic, Slobodan Cvijetic, Eugene O'Sullivan, and Ms. Tatjana Savic appearing for Stanisic Defence this morning. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Dragan Krgovic and Miroslav Cuskic appearing for the Zupljanin Defence. Mr. Zupljanin is not present; he signed a waiver.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Zecevic, we are advised that you have a matter to raise.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, there is one preliminary matter which I wanted to raise with Your Honours at the end of yesterday's session. I stood up and I was having an objection. In the meantime, I consulted with my friend Ms. Korner from the Prosecution side, and I withdraw that objection. But there is one other matter that I wanted to raise the attention of the Trial Chamber to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Namely, the document P400 and the part which was read by Ms. Korner to the witness contains a mistake in English translation on page 21 of the document in e-court. Namely, instead of putting it in the first -- in the -- first person like it is in the translation, it should be -- it should be "they." So the plural and -- in a very general. So what we are going to do is we will ask the -- send the document to CLSS for verification of translation. That is all I wanted to raise with Your Honours. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, I certainly won't pursue the line of questioning until that's sorted out, I may say it's unfortunate because it's obviously something that the Prosecution have been relying on since the beginning of the case, that it hasn't been spotted before, but there's not much I can do about that now. I don't believe I have very much time left.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: I was about to remind you that you have exhausted your time.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, I was going to ask, Your Honours, in that case, I wasn't go to get through any more documents, but I need to deal with two matters that he has been raising. Firstly, this document that he says is this order by Subotic which gives the military the control over everything which is actually one of the documents that was in my binder and I didn't use because I wondered how he was able to quote so accurately the number of the document, and he must have seen it when he was reading through them, but I feel I ought to go back and just deal with that. That's the first thing. Second thing, there's one matter that he spoke about yesterday which I want to go back on and just deal with in the question of his knowledge of who was involved in these 300 people who were in prison. So if I can have time to do that. The last matter is this: As Your Honour will have seen, as with so many of these witnesses, getting an answer to a question is -- that you've asked, is very difficult; but I don't want to stop them - Mr. Cvijetic says that is what I'm doing - even if they are going right off track too often. But it does eat into the time that I've been allowed. Accordingly, can I just mention that one of the documents I intended to ask him about was the January 1993 Assembly meeting which he attended even though he was no longer the minister. I obviously haven't got time to do that. Can I just, as it were, as somebody in my jurisdiction keeps saying, put down a marker that he is probably the last witness I could directly deal with the Assembly. It's got important stuff in it, but it will have to be one of the documents that we apply to put in via a bar table motion. So if I can just -- because I can't deal with it through him; I haven't got time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: And in terms of the two issues with which you would --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: They're both quite short.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: The -- my question was, How long would these two items take?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: If I can get him just to answer, you know, very quickly, then it shouldn't take more than ten minutes absolute max.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, I remind you, you are still on your oath. Yes, Ms. Korner, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, I've got two very short matters I want to deal with this morning and then you will be cross-examined. The first is this: You told the Trial Chamber -- I'll just find it. Yesterday you recall I was asking you about when you were saying to Mr. Krajisnik the 400 prisoners. And I asked you whether the 400 people -- were they civilians, and you said, "I don't know, Madam Prosecutor, I don't know who those people were." And in fairness to you, Mr. Mandic, because this is even further on from the time that we are talking about than in Krajisnik, can I just remind you of what you said in Krajisnik, and you said that -- to the Court that other than the changes you made, you stood by what you said. And this is at page 8886, which was day four of your testimony. This was questioning by Judge Orie. At the top of page 8886. He says: "Mr. Mandic, I'm interested in the 400 people that were in Kula as you told us. Were they men, women, children? What was the composition? More or less, not in detail, of course?" And you replied: "I think that there were men, women, and children, Your Honour." Do you remember saying that?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember, but I don't have any doubts that it is formulated as you have just read it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And then Judge Orie went: "Ages?" And you said: "That was a long time ago. It's difficult for me to remember. But I do know that they had come from the Dobrinja neighbourhood, that they had been frightened, and that they wanted to leave that area." Judge Orie said: "Yes. Were they exchanged?" And you said: "No, Your Honours. On my own initiative, and with the approval of Mico Stanisic and Tepavcevic, who were the heads of police, took those people to the Vrbanja Most."

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do you want me to explain what this was all about now that you have reminded me? Had there been no exchange, the people were taken to the part of the town held by Muslims. This is what I said in the Krajisnik case. Therefore, there was no exchange. People were simply sent to the Vrbanja Bridge, the part of Sarajevo that was Muslim controlled. And those were residents of Dobrinje that sought shelter from war operations. And it was a mixture, men, women, and children. There were fierce fighting in the part of Sarajevo where these population found themselves in. So no exchange took place. These people were just removed from the combat zone.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Mandic, that's fine. You did explain it all in the Krajisnik testimony, as you said. I just wanted to remind you because you said you didn't know yesterday. The other matter is the document --

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just one minute. We spoke yesterday about the 400 people who had had come from Hadzici. It's probably a different group of people, not the one from Dobrinje neighbourhood. There may have been a mix between these two groups.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Mr. Mandic, believe you me, all your evidence in -- that you gave in Krajisnik is before the Trial Chamber, so we don't have to repeat it. But I want to ask you about this question of this order from Subotic that you spoke about twice yesterday, and, indeed, you gave the actual number, and I think that was because you had some notes and you made a note of some of the documents you looked at; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You are talking about yesterday?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, no, I was just a little bit nervous and I was just signing my name on the piece of paper.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, you see, you actually, yesterday - this is at page 9537 - when I was asking you about the -- the document which was at 2650 about Mr. Poplasen asking for detainees to be used for construction. And you said at the top of page 9537: "There are documents indicating that nobody else except the military commander was authorised to send non-Serbs to perform labour. This was an order published in the Official Gazette 6/92, signed by Bogdan Subotic." I believe at that stage you actually had a note of that document, didn't you? Or did you just recall exactly what the number was?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Madam Prosecutor. This order was part of my case when I was being tried in the Bosnia-Herzegovina court. I remember clearly about that when I presented my own defence. What I did yesterday was just writing down my signature. I was not taking any notes. And I can say that I know this order of Mr. Subotic by heart because it was crucial to my trial.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Quite. All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Could we have a look at that order. Document P189, please. Which is tab 67 in our binder.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, that's the one.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. This, as you say, is published in the gazette on the 13th of June, 1992. Instructions on the treatment of captured persons.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And can we go to the second page, please, in the English. And the third page -- sorry, fourth page in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And there we see it's signed minister of the defence Colonel Subotic, and again the date of the 13th of June, Order 26, 1992?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, can we go back to the first page, please, in each. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Instructions on the treatment of captured persons. These instructions set out the rights and duties of military personnel of the army and members of the Serbian Ministry of Internal Affairs relative to the treatment of captured persons. And then it defines, does it not, in paragraph 2: "Captured persons shall be taken to mean the members of the enemy armed forces who have surrendered and laid down their arms or who -- or have been overpowered in or out of combat." Correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And then in paragraph 10, which is on the same page in English but -- and the third page in the B/C/S, besides work connected with the cleaning and maintenance of the camp, captured persons may be put to work in agriculture, industry, mining, handycrafts, traffic trade, and other areas which are not directly related to war operations." Is that the part you were thinking of?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This entire instruction relates to the army. The minister of defence is now instructing the army how to treat the captives. Captives involved both military personnel and civilians who are captured. It is true that he is giving instructions to military officers how to use the captured persons for performing the work outside the camp. So this refers exclusively to the army, not to the police or the Ministry of Justice relating to exploitation, release, and capture. So there's no categorisation here whatsoever, whether there were civilians or military personnel, he is just talking about captives here. And this is the minister of defence. He is giving instructions to the army. He is not authorised to give any instructions to the police or anybody else.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Absolutely, Mr. Mandic, and I think you've made the point that I was trying to make. These instructions, as you say, apply only to the army, because he has no authority to give them to anybody else, and apply only to those who are captives, captured persons, as defined in paragraph 2; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you very much, Mr. Mandic. That's all that I ask.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Madam Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Mandic.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning. Good luck to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: At the beginning of your questioning on Monday, my learned friend Ms. Korner asked you about the changes in your testimony in the Krajisnik case that you made by giving a statement to the OTP on the 25th of March, 2010, here in The Hague. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: The first alteration relates to the explanation of the 10.000 people who all were in the Butmir camp. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: On page --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the counsel please repeat again the page and the line.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic and Mr. Mandic, I understand that a part of the problem has been that the witness, Mr. Mandic, in his examination-in-chief had been speaking a little too quickly for the interpreters and, of course, Mr. Mandic, you, I would remind you and Mr. Zecevic that inasmuch as you speak the same language, it is especially necessary in cross-examination for both of you to slow down and to allow that interval between the question and the answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I understand, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The interpreters said they didn't hear the page number.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll repeat.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: So my question was: On page 9402, line 17 of the transcript of Monday, your answer to the question Ms. Korner asked you about this alteration of your statement was entered, but I don't think it was translated in its entirety. The way I understood you, on Monday you said that during your evidence in the Krajisnik case you explained the situation and that you heard that while you were listening to the tapes during the proofing for this testimony, but you had forgotten you had already changed that in the Krajisnik case. Is my understanding correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The figure of 10.000 people was mentioned in my testimony in the Krajisnik case when a letter was shown to me written by Ljubica Vladosic and Dragan Bulajic who requested assistance and food for KPD Butmir. In that letter, it is said that about 10.000 people had been processed at that KPD. Then I accepted that number, that 10.000 people had been processed there, but not as prisoners or captives, but, rather, as persons who were exchanged there, because that was the place where the state commission of both the Serbian entity and the Muslim entity exchanged people. That was a place where people sought shelter from combat activities in the immediate vicinity, and that's the Dobrinje neighbourhood where there's the Sarajevo airport. And the third reason for this large throughput of people was that on the premises of the pre-war prison, there was a large chicken farm where people came and got food to survive, because there was a shortage of food. And I said that in that context. I didn't mean people who were taken prisoner. And that's what I repeated on Monday, and I said as much in the Krajisnik case.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The second alteration you spoke about in your statement given on the 25th of March, 2010, and also on Monday at the beginning of your examination related to the duration of detention. In your evidence it is recorded 30 days, as Ms. Korner put to you, but you corrected that because under the law police can impose detention for up to three days. And after that the person in question must be taken to an investigating judge who has the authority to extend the detention for up to 30 days and in certain cases up to six months until an indictment is issued, right?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Both the Prosecutor and I agreed that this is possibly a mistake, the only mistake. Why? Because, under the laws in force then about criminal procedure, in former Yugoslavia there was the rule that the police can detain a person up to 72 hours, which means up to three days. This was obviously a mistake. But another observation of mine about a mistake. Yesterday at a certain moment the Prosecutor showed us the proposal for the police to extend a detention for up to 21 days, but that probably was not adopted. So if the duration of detention was up to 30 days, it's not logical for them to propose an extension for up to 21 days because one excludes the other.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: That would have been my following question. I will later show you a report of the MUP from July 1992 which was sent to the president of the Presidency and the prime minister and it contains this proposal that the duration of detention be extended up to 21 days. I'll show you that later. Be that as it may, that proposal was not adopted or even discussed so that the situation with regard to the duration of detention that can be imposed by the police remained as it had been under the law until that time which is up to 72 hours; correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Finally, on page 9408, you were explaining, prompted by a question by the Prosecutor, your third alteration that relates to Mr. Mico Stanisic. It's a fact, isn't it, that after the Defence at our meeting on the 21st of March this year in The Hague put to you that our client has nothing to do with the dispatch of May 1992, you said that our allegation is correct and that what we say is true; is that so?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. And I explained to the Trial Chamber what happened. We don't need to repeat that. I also said the same to the Prosecutor during the proofing.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I don't want to repeat, but we need it for the transcript. You stated the reasons to us why that mistake was made during the testimony in the Krajisnik trial and then you put forward the same reasons as here in your statement on the 25th of March, 2010. Then in the proofing note that you made before your testimony on Monday, because the Prosecution also asked you about that, and also during your testimony on Monday you always stated the identical reasons?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And they are the true reasons, the real reasons.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, if you are going to put the proofing note to him, then you should put the full thing that he said.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm not going to put to the witness the proofing note.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, but you've just said: "... in the proofing note that you made before testimony ... you stated the identical reasons." He gave extra reasons, Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, you see, Mr. Mandic, I still have to read it to you. We have to go through it. Your proofing note dated the 3rd of May, 2010, is the conversation you had with Ms. Korner and an investigator of this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know, Your Honours, if this document is in e-court. If so, we can show it on the screens.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I wouldn't have thought so, Your Honours. Sorry, I wouldn't have thought so, Your Honour, because a proofing note is a summary of what the witness said. It's not a word-for-word record of the conversation. So, I mean, as such, I don't know that it's ever become -- it shouldn't be part of evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Can we put it on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: We can put it on -- on Sanction, Your Honours. Your Honours should have had a copy. It was sent to the Legal Officers.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, for the very reason that Ms. Korner has mentioned, this being a summary of the witness's statement and the summary was made by an investigator and someone from the OTP is why I didn't want to read it out. But Ms. Korner insisted that the proofing note be read. Now, I expect instructions from the Bench with regard what I should do.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, can I just say, at the beginning of the proofing note it relates to the matter that you had -- that Mr. Mandic raised but which was in private session. So it should probably not be displayed to the general public at the moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: While you're on your feet, Ms. Korner, did I understand you to be, as Mr. Zecevic understands your position, that the proofing note, the entire proofing note, should be read? I didn't understand that to be your position.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, no. No, no. Mr. Zecevic said to him, In the proofing note you gave exactly the same reasons for why you had changed your testimony. I said he gave additional reasons. And that the only -- it's the additional reason that he gave that should be put to him. If that's what -- I mean, the assertion that Mr. Zecevic made is just slightly inaccurate, that's all. That's all I was saying.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: So, Mr. Zecevic, it seems that it would be sufficient for you to put the relevant passage in the proofing note to set the context for the contradiction you are suggesting the witness has made. That will be sufficient.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I understand, Your Honours, and I will read the passage of the proofing note.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Mandic, this says that during your proofing at the Prosecution on the 3rd of May, 2010, you said the following. I will read it in English: "He said that it didn't seem to matter how this had come about when he was testifying against Krajisnik. And it had seemed logical that it was MS, but ongoing through the transcript he realised he had heard about the law being enacted from Ostojic and had sent the dispatch on his own initiative. Now that MS was on trial, although he was not protecting MS," meaning Mico Stanisic, "he did not want to say it was him. MS has four children." [Interpretation] This is how it was recorded by the OTP. I suppose that Ms. Korner, in her objection, is alluding to what was mentioned here as Mico Stanisic having four children?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yesterday when I started giving evidence, I clearly explained my mistake, the mistake I made involving the names of the people who had co-operated with me with regard to the dispatch. I didn't want anybody to suffer harm due to my mistake. I mentioned these four children, but -- because I didn't want to wrong the man, because he had nothing to do with the dispatch. And I explained as much on Monday.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I believe that we have thus exhausted this topic. You gave us an explanation. All the other reasons have been repeated several times in your statement and during your testimony here and also in the interview with us on the 21st of March, 2010. Let's move on. On Monday while you were giving evidence, on page 9411, you said that Mico Stanisic remained minister of the interior of the Republic of Serbian Bosnia-Herzegovina, that being the name then, ad hoc because for Vitomir Zepinic who had been appointed minister of the interior earlier, and that decision had been published in the Official Gazette, it had been established that he was involved in illegal activity, and that is why Mico Stanisic was appointed. Do you remember saying that?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and that is true.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: My learned friend Ms. Korner, on page 9413, said that she would return to this issue to clarify, but she didn't, hence we will. When you said that the appointment of Vitomir Zepinic for minister of the interior of the Republic of Serbian Bosnia-Herzegovina, you meant document P180.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If we can see it on our screens, please, in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Tab number?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I am sorry, I don't have a tab number for this one.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can see it on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: 207. Ms. Korner, tab 207.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, this is page 10 of the Official Gazette of the Serbian people in Bosnia-Herzegovina. That is the Official Gazette. Issue 1, dated Wednesday, the 15th of January, 1992. And under 22, there's the decision on the establishment and election of the Ministerial Council of the Assembly of the Serbian people in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Under Roman numeral III, and I believe that is the following page in -- of the English document, it says: "The following members of the ministerial council are appointed ministers:" And under number 1 we see Ranko Nikolic at minister for judicial and administrative matters, and under number 2, Dr. Vitomir Zepinic as minister of the interior.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe I explained that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Under 18 there's the name of Mr. Mico Stanisic and it says, As minister without portfolio. During your examination on Monday you said that in January it was published that Vitomir Zepinic had been appointed minister of the interior of Republika Srpska; you meant this very document, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: During your testimony both in the Krajisnik trial and yesterday and the day before yesterday and this trial, you mentioned Mr. Ranko Nikolic, minister of justice and public administration, who didn't turn up to take his position and that's why you became minister of justice and public administration, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, let me ask you this: This Official Gazette of the Serbian people in Bosnia-Herzegovina, this issue number 1 dated 15 January 1992, was some sort of confidential, secret document?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it was published in the Official Gazette, a publication in the public domain. And it says that it would be published in the Official Gazette of the Serbian people of Bosnia-Herzegovina. It's line four.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vitomir Zepinic - it says at the bottom of the decision that it was made on the 21st December, 1991, but it was published in the Official Gazette on the 15th of January - so Mr. Vitomir Zepinic was then appointed minister of the interior and simultaneously he discharged the duties of the deputy minister of the interior of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, that is, deputy to minister Alija Delimustafic, all the way up to the end of the war?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Until April 1992 when he resigned to that post, and he was the highest ranking official of Serb ethnicity in the Ministry of the Interior.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I believe you said until 4 April 1992 when he resigned to the post?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, deputy minister of the joint MUP. And until then he was the highest ranking official of Serb ethnicity in the joint MUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: We need to avoid overlapping, really, so that the interpreters can keep pace. If I understood your testimony correctly, your evidence in this trial and in the Krajisnik trial, at that time in March and early April 1992, it was established beyond any doubt that Mr. Zepinic was involved in some unlawful activities, and I think you said a car had been found, Mazda 626, along with the addresses of official -- sorry, the offices given Zepinic by the democratic action party?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the address where the car was found and the address where those offices were registered in the name of his wife, Milosava. Shall I give you these addresses again? The offices were in Lenin Street 67, next to the Bosko Buha Kindergarten. It was over 100 square metres. And the car, Mazda 626, was found by the police, the chief of which was Tomo Kovac, at an address in Kasindol. And we didn't find the money.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I would like to go through our transcript now and clear up certain matters and discuss again some of the documents that the Prosecution had shown you over the past few days. On page 9415 when you were explaining the decision of the Trial Chamber considering charges against you for embezzlement, your complete explanation was not recorded, so I would like to correct that. If I understood you well, you said at the time that there is no precedent in the legal practice of any country whatsoever, that anyone can embezzle their own money, and that is why you claim that this judgement was unfair.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and I can explain.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Take it easy, please.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said at the beginning to the Trial Chamber when I was explaining the treatment that I had received when attempting to enter the European Union on this occasion. In 1993 I was black-listed, that is, entry was forbidden to me into the United States and the European Union on the grounds that I was suspected of helping the hiding of Dr. Radovan Karadzic and helping to finance it. I had been detained in Serbia on those suspicions, and Serbia has not apologised to me to this day. And I was also tried before a court in Bosnia and Herzegovina. In this trial, a final decision, a final judgement, acquitted me of those charges. In the same trial, I was, however, convicted of abuse of authority. And Your Honours know that this crime does not exist in democratic societies. It's only when there's nothing else to pin on the person that this crime is claimed. And I was convicted because I gave loans as director of a bank to certain companies that were suspected of helping the hiding of Radovan Karadzic and they failed to return these loans. I was convicted on the basis of false testimony by an American citizen, Tony Robinson -- or Toby Robinson. Later on, it was established that these loans were non-existent. In fact, these loans and the money are my property. And when I was there before the court, I asked, To whom I should pay damages. They said, The owner of Privredna Banka. And when I said that I am the owner of Privredna Banka so I had no one to pay damages to, they had no answer. Therefore, I had been detained solely on the grounds of suspicions that were never proven, and that is my grudge. And the director of the IMF and the World Bank for Development and Reconstruction would have to be in prison for millions of years if they were convicted for writing off loans to countries that are obviously unable to repay them.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let us now return to some documents shown to you by Ms. Korner. In the course of examination-in-chief the day before yesterday and yesterday, Ms. Korner showed you some documents and asked you to comment. I classified these under three general topics that Ms. Korner has dealt with. Let's start with group number 1. Ms. Korner asked you to comment on speeches during Assembly meetings made by some MPs whom you designated as extremist; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, you are not a politician, are you?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm not.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: However, members of parliament were elected in free elections?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, by direct ballot in a perfectly democratic way. That's how MPs are chosen.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And MPs are ultimately responsible for whatever they say in the Assembly to their own voters, and that is why they enjoy immunity as members of parliament?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is standard practice and that is what the law envisages throughout the world. We members of executive authority, people who were of the same mind as I who had the best intentions to introduce and impose the rule of law, encountered many problems in our attempts and efforts. These extremists would confront us and oppose us and draw along many other MPs. I refrain from telling people like them that they were wrong. I instead wrote letters asking that local authorities be reflective of the ethnic structure of a given area. But MPs of that kind would make speeches and elicit support from others, saying things along the lines of it's a disgrace if you don't support your own. However, at my insistence, the insistence of Mr. Karadzic and Mr. Djeric, in most of the cases my idea that the ethnic structure of the judiciary should reflect the ethnic structure of a given area succeeded.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, could I ask you to give me concise answers and focus on my questions in order not to waste time, because my time is limited as was Ms. Korner's. Let us go back to Assembly sessions. The Assembly has its own rules, including disciplinary measures applicable to MPs, and these rules are written in the Rules of Procedure of the Assembly, and various other regulatory provisions applying to the Assembly?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: You participated in those Assembly sessions as a member of the cabinet?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, as a member of the cabinet, I attended some Assembly sessions.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: The government, the cabinet, is an organ of the Assembly?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And the government answers for its work to the Assembly?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. The Assembly elects and replaces the government.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, the Prosecution asked you why you had failed to react when you did not agree with the arguments of various MPs. Isn't it a fact that you, as a member of the government, were unable to speak at Assembly sessions even if you wished to unless a question is directed to you by MPs concerning items on the agenda that concern your ministry directly? Isn't it a fact that you were unable to take part in parliamentary debates?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When the issue of the election of these judiciary officials was discussed, it is a fact that I had no right to speak.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And this particular limitation applies to all members of the government and all ministers, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: On yesterday's transcript, page 9486, Ms. Korner discussed with you an intercept in which you talked to Prstojevic. That's 65 ter 3256. Prstojevic was in Ilidza and you were reasoning with him and trying to persuade him not to drive out members of other ethnic groups from the territory of the municipality. You were telling him it is the position of the government and it was your policy. And then on page 9487, you said to Ms. Korner that there were many such people as Prstojevic in some smaller places, namely people who advocated very extreme views. Do you remember saying that?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: It is a fact that in some of those smaller places individuals of that sort ran out of control completely, as it were, and you said yesterday they were practically creating their own little states?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it's typical of Serb people.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: It is a fact, isn't it, that as a result of the war in 1992, the central government in Republika Srpska was not easy and quick to establish. There were no mechanisms of central authority?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As the conflict escalated, communications broke down. Both telecommunications and roads were cut off, and it was very difficult to keep in touch with all the territories held by Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: It's also a fact, isn't it, that this lack of control and that this parochial conduct of some local Mandarins was noticed as a problem very early on, and even back on 23rd May, 1992, it was suggested at a government meeting that Crisis Staffs should be abolished?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and a decision was made to abolish them.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's P217, tab 39. Could we call that document up.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: This is under item 4. Do you agree, Mr. Mandic?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: That was the 23rd of May session. You were at the time already the minister of judiciary in that cabinet, and a conclusion was reached to undertake measures to abolish Crisis Staffs; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: It is a fact, isn't it, Mr. Mandic, that due to inability of the central government to control the territory, attempts were made to contemplate and to draw up various alternatives to the Crisis Staffs that eventually turned out to be a huge problem?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. One of the alternatives was -- just like Mr. Poplasen was in Vogosca - I don't know how it was called - I think it was called commissioners for certain towns that were appointed by the Presidency of Republika Srpska. That was a transitional solution pending total abolishment of the local authorities and stripping them of all their jurisdiction.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm going to remind you that there were War Presidencies and then war commissioner's offices were in place after that; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And this, as you put it, abolishment of local authorities took place in September 1992 following the adoption of the amendment to the constitution of Republika Srpska and some subsequent decisions?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, it is a fact that the corridor in Northern Bosnia was opened only in early July 1992; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That was a huge problem for the Serbian people. It is well known that tens of babies died in the maternity ward in the hospital in Banja Luka due to the lack of medicine. This caused outrage among the Serbian people in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: It is also a fact, isn't it, Mr. Mandic, that for a certain period of time until this corridor was opened, neither the government nor the ministries had almost no information about what was happening in northwestern Bosnia, which is the territory of the Krajina, as well as in central Bosnia, that is to say, Doboj, Brcko, and Samac; Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I explained that all telecommunications and road communications were severed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we just -- on page 25, line 12, I said Doboj, Brcko, and Samac. Can that please be corrected in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: As the government, and you as the minister, received information about what was happening in that period -- in that area, the Northern Bosnia, north of Posavina, only in July 1992; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: On page 9494 of yesterday's transcript, you were shown document P427.11.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please have it in e-court. 427.11.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: This relates to the 28th session of the Government of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina held on the 15th of June, 1992. You remember that you discussed this document with Ms. Korner?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: On page 4, I think both in Serbian and English, we have item 10. My learned friend asked you about the commission that was set up and was tasked with reviewing certain information arriving from the ground concerning the exchange of prisoners, et cetera. You said that it also involved the bringing in of civilians into illegal prisons, wrongful arrests, et cetera. You remember that?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but can I see the proper page. Yes, it's okay now.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: You can see, it's under item 10.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: It is a fact, isn't it, that this commission and the information provided to you at the time, that is to say, on 15th of June, 1992, did not cover part of the territory that we discussed a moment ago, that is to say, you had no information whatsoever at the time?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: In other words, this commission was set up based on the information arriving from parts of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina with which you had communications?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: On page 9559 of yesterday's transcript, you confirmed in response to Ms. Korner's question that you had no information about Manjaca and Sanski Most; do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. I had no information whatsoever. We simply couldn't obtain any information because the Krajina was completely severed. Only after the corridor had been opened, we could use the roads and telecommunications.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Although your ministry had certain institutions on the ground that were under your jurisdictions, like, for example, the prison in Doboj, the district prison in Doboj, you had no contact with that institution all the way until the corridor was opened; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, due to these and similar problems, I think that Doboj was set up only towards the end of 1992 in December after we had completed the re-organisation and established the job qualification, adopted rules of governance, and we only appointed the governor of the prison towards the end of 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: The fact is that after you learned about the events that had taken place in those territories that became accessible to you after July 1992, the Government of Republika Srpska adopted, on 9th of August, 1992, a decision to set up a commission which will visit all the collection centres and other detention centres where prisoners were kept in the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. That's 65 ter 1422.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I'm being warned about this document, that it was on the Prosecution 65 ter list but that it had been removed from the list on the 14th of April of this year pursuant to a ruling. At that time, we notified the Registrar about this and we talked with Mr. Philip, and it was suggested to us not to upload this document for a second time since it's already in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry, could I have an explanation of that. I'm not sure what you are talking about. Are you saying this is a document we removed as a result of a ruling by the Trial Chamber?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: That is my understanding. The ruling of the --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, I see the time. Yes, I'm not clear at the moment on what basis. If you ordered us to take it off, it's going back in again. If Your Honours take the break, I can discuss it with Mr. Zecevic and maybe we can sort this out.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, maybe that would be the best.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, we'll take the break now.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, while we are waiting for the witness to come in, may I just remind Your Honours that the discussion we had on Monday morning, we need to notify VWS as to when the next witness should be brought up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: We haven't forgotten, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: May I continue, Your Honours?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please have 65 ter 1422 in e-court, please. 65 ter 1422. Page 2 in both versions.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Finally we have the document, Mr. Mandic, on our screens. As I said, this is a decision by the government to form a commission. The decision was taken on the 9th of August, 1992, on behalf of the government. It was signed by Mr. Trbojevic. Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Pursuant to this decision, the government, in fact, set up two commissions to visit the collection centres. One commission, under A, Vojin Lale and Mirko Erkic; and under B we have Slobodan Avlijas and Goran Saric. Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And under item 2, the government tasked the commission in detail, pursuant to this decision. Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Under item 3, the commission instructed -- was instructed to submit reports following the inspections?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: You have seen this before?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If there are no objections, I would like to tender this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit 1D254, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, this commission was not the commission of your ministry, but, rather, a commission set up by the government; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was the government commission made up of experts in this particular area.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: These two commissions submitted their respective reports in relation to the territories they had visited. The commission, under A, made up of Vojin Lale and Mirko Erkic, submitted a report, P194 dated the 17th of August, 1992. The report was submitted to the government, and it reads that this is a report by the commission, following the inspection of prisoner facilities in the region of Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please have Exhibit P194.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: You can see this front page, and do you remember this report?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Since this is a document already in evidence, let us not waste time. Based on this report and the report submitted by commission B, the government received an aggregate report shown to you yesterday which was marked P393, summarising these two reports?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: All right. And all these reports, as we said, went to the government because it was a government commission; right?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let us pass on to something else. Or, rather, one more question. Only based on the findings of these commissions that were submitted in the second half of August, the government, including the ministries, received a comprehensive picture of the situation in the territories visited by the commissions?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they were informed of the situation on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When you say "situation on the ground," you mean the situation with regard to the matters with which the commissions were tasked?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Let us pass on to the second group of questions my learned friend Ms. Korner asked you in the two days of examination-in-chief. This second group of questions related to prisoners, commissions for exchange, imprisonment facilities, et cetera. Even today she asked you again about something similar. On page 9499 of the transcript, you spoke about the authorities with regard to the prisoners and the powers of the military commanders with regard to that. Do you remember?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: An instruction was mentioned about the treatment of prisoners, dated the 13th of June, 1992, which was drafted and published in the Official Gazette by the Ministry of Defence -- or the Minister of Defence Subotic. We saw it. P427.27. Let us take a look at it again and explain some of the facts. This is the instruction on the treatment of captured persons which you saw at the beginning of today's hearing. Do you remember?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Ms. Korner quoted some of the items to you, I believe it was item 2, item 10, et cetera. I would like us to comment on item 4. Item 4 reads that: "Captured persons shall be taken to reception centres as determined by a senior officer with the rank of company commander or by a person holding an equal or higher position before the start of combat activities." Can you see it?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Which means that the military, before it launches a military operation, the officer, that is, the company commander or higher-ranking officer, depending on who is in charge of the operation, determines the place to be considered a reception centre; right?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And then in the following paragraph of the same item, we read: "After their identity has been established in the reception centre, captured persons shall be taken to prison camp in an organised manner and under escort." Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now see the following page of the Serbian text, and I believe we can stay on the same page of the English version. The items I'm interested in are 12, 17, 18, and 19. Page 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: You see that it says in item 12 that: "The camp commander shall issue regulations relative to specific rights and obligations of captured persons, their behaviour in the camp, and the conditions for the application of disciplinary measures. The regulations shall be displayed publicly so that all captured persons can see them." Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is exactly what I tried to explain, having been asked by the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And the last thing. Item 18 reads: "The commanders of corps of they Army of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina are responsible for ..." In the English version this on the following page, item 18, et cetera. It is signed by Minister of Defence Colonel Bogdan Subotic; right?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is what I was saying, the corps commanders were deciding on who was to be released and who was to be kept, who was to be considered a POW, and, again, this was applied to all captured persons, both military staff and civilians, non-Serbs. Only the corps commander had the power to decide on these matters. And this instruction with legal force was published in the Official Gazette of the Serbian People. Since there was an imminent threat of war, this had legal force and was binding for both the military and the civilian authorities, including the police and everybody else.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: It's a fact, isn't it, sir, that under Article 4 of the Geneva Convention on the treatment of prisoners -- or let me put it this way, Article 4 of the Geneva Convention on the Rights of Prisoners of War lists all those persons that are to be considered prisoners of war under the convention. There are six times plus two additional items. Are you familiar with that?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: You will agree with me when I say, I hope, that a person - and this in line with the provisions of the Geneva Convention - gets the status of a prisoner of war as from the moment it comes under the control of the enemy?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, if it happened in combat and if that person was armed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: That means if the military carries out some operation and takes some persons prisoner - and in this instruction we see -- we read "captured persons." From that moment on, those persons are under the control of the military that took them prisoner?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Under the authority of the military commander with territorial jurisdiction.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Certainly as the commander under this instruction before commencing the operation must decide what is to be considered a collection centre and once the persons have been brought there after the military operation, a certain procedure must be applied to establish whether or not a certain person meets the conditions to be considered a POW of the Geneva Convention; right?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is in line with the instruction and it's in accordance with the standards of the Geneva Convention.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: That means until the moment this procedure is carried out and until it is established whether those persons have a status under the Geneva Convention or whether they are civilians or have some other status, they remain in that collection centre or in that facility under the control of the military; right?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They remain under the control of the military, but they are captured persons. Once that procedure is carried out, then it is established who is a soldier, who is a civilian, et cetera. It's done by the relevant services, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In your 92 ter package, there's document 65 ter 1403 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic, are you moving on to something else? Because I have a few questions relating to this document and this matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was it was my intention to move on, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Then can I just kick in a few questions. First of all, Mr. Mandic, the instruction that we saw to set up the reception centres did not, as I could see, make the distinction between POWs and civilians. It just said that the identity had to be established of the captive person, and then once that procedure had been brought to an end, the person was then to be passed on to, I think the term was, prison camps. So my question is: What would the commander do if he sat in front of a captured person and that person turned out to be a civilian? Would that person then still be sent to a prison camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, this is about captive persons, and civilians are not distinguished from military prisoners of war. Once the relevant services establish who was a civilian and who isn't, they classify the persons in accordance with military rules and decide where these persons are to be put up. And this depended exclusively on the corps commander and his services.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Yes, I can read that in the rule or in the instruction. But my question to you was that the rule in paragraph 4 only said that the captive persons would be passed on or sent on to prison camps. And so I repeat my question: Since the rule itself does not make any distinction between prison camp for prisoners of war and other detention facilities for civilians, then it looks to me as if everybody, prisoners of war as well as civilians, would be sent to the same prison camps?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Whether they were sent to separate camps or the same ones as it says here, I cannot tell you, Your Honour, because I had no knowledge about that. Those camps were secured by the army, and the army ran those camps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: But, Mr. Mandic, you being the minister of justice at the time, you would have taken part in the government's considerations about how to treat all of these people. So what was your input to the issue of how to treat civilians who for one reason or another had been detained?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is contained in the report of the government commission on the proposed measures. It was submitted to both the president of the republic and the cabinet and all relevant institutions. Because the governmental commission, which was composed of experts and had visited various parts of the territory controlled by the Bosnian Serbs, drafted a report on the conditions in those camps and made proposals as to the measures which should be done in those camps where civilians, women and children, and POWs were held. This is a already an exhibit in this trial. Because a civilian body of state administration could only propose measures for the army to implement or those who controlled those camps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: And so the camps that were set up to hold the civilians, would they come under the jurisdiction of the Ministry of Justice?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour. The Ministry of Justice set up prisons and facilities for penitentiary facilities for the needs of the judicial system of Republika Srpska. This has nothing to do with the camps in which non-Serbs were kept. These are two completely separate institutions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Forgive me for trying to explore this further on. We have been through this issue with many witnesses before you, Mr. Mandic. I'm simply trying to get a better understanding of just how this was done. Let's get back to the starting point. As far as prisoners of war are concerned, they would be held in special prison camps run by the Ministry of Defence; did I get that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Right. If then civilians were detained, then they would first be sent to a reception centre where their identity would be established and in -- more particularly, their role of being either a combatant or a non-combatant. So if --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: If the reception centre established that the person was not a combatant, that is to say, a civilian, then he or she would be sent to a separate camp; is that correct? Separate from the camp that would hold the prisoners of war. Is that correctly understood?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Reading and trying to interpret this instruction, that's what it says. However, both captured civilians and POWs were the responsibility of the army because they were detained and released on account of war and during the war, and there was no other institution with jurisdiction and authority to detain or release them apart from the army. And that is pursuant to this instruction and on the orders of the President of the Republic Dr. Karadzic. Because this here is preceded by an order which I see is not included in this material.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Well, my concern is still that civilians who were captured and detained would ordinarily be detained under the authority of either the Ministry of Justice or the Ministry of the Interior, but certainly not by the army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was only under the jurisdiction of the army because nobody could be under the jurisdiction of the Ministry of Justice unless an investigating judge had made a decision to detain a civilian on account of a criminal offence, because the Ministry of Justice as a state organ had no authority to detain anyone during the war unless it was doing a service for the army or following a decision of a competent court in the area, because the Ministry of Justice established penal correctional facilities only in July and early August, and that process continued until December that year, from all I know from my term in office as minister.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, maybe I could ask you a different question or, rather, ask you a question from a different angle, namely to say, was there in the government a clear plan of how to deal with all the various categories of persons who were detained during the war in the summer of 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. In August and September, commissions were established and a plan was adopted to close down collection centres set up by local Crisis Staffs that were spread all over the territory and with which the government had no communication, as it had no communication with certain areas held by Serbs. That's why these commissions were set up and prepared a comprehensive report on how to close down these camps where people were detained, civilian or non-civilian. The government, the Presidency of the republic, and the Supreme Command of the army were all informed of this, and they were the only ones who were able to take the necessary steps because the Ministry of Justice or the Ministry of the Interior as organs of state authority were unable to do anything about detained non-Serbs in circumvention of the army because the immediate state of -- the immediate threat of war had been proclaimed, and we had to act pursuant to this instruction issued by the minister of defence. It was published in the Official Gazette and had the force of law. And this clearly says that local army commanders have jurisdiction over detained people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: So, if I understand you correctly, in the end the responsibility for all categories of captured persons during the war was left in the hands of the army; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: May I proceed, Your Honours?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Back to you, Mr. Zecevic. Thanks.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I may be of assistance, I believe when the witness was speaking about the commission of the -- of the report of the commission, referred to 5393 -- sorry, P393. It's a report made by the state commission proposing certain measures that needed to be applied.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's precisely what I tried to explain to the Court. The government could only propose measures, but it could not enforce them. It could only propose how to close down these illegal prisons and to put everything in conformity with the rule of law, and that could only be implemented by army commanders at the local level.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Mandic. Let us go back to your 92 ter packet, 65 ter 1403. It's a letter from the state commission. Tab 35. It's from the 92 ter package. I'm not sure you received it. It's a letter on whose page 3 you will see the President of the State Commission Filip Vukovic. It concerns the state commission for the exchange of prisoners on the side of the Federation. And you talked about it in your direct examination?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: He didn't. I didn't ask him about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I said you mentioned the name of Filip Vukovic in regard to an intercept. I believe it was a conversation with Krajisnik, do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I'm looking at Madam Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honours, I shouldn't have interrupted. I thought it was suggested that I showed him this document, but I hadn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Very briefly, sir. Considering that there was a state commission in the Federation headed by this Filip Vukovic, it means, doesn't it, that the other side also captured Serbs?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And it was precisely these captives who were exchanged for persons captured in the military operations of the Army of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Another document on the same issue from your 1992 ter package, tab 32, P179.18. It's a government decision dated 8 May 1992. It's a decision to establish a central government commission for the exchange of prisoners of war, arrested persons, and bodies of the dead. It was headed by Rajko Colovic?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: On page 2 we see the signature of the prime minister, Dr. Branko Djeric. It's a fact, isn't it, that this central commission was also a government commission?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And it had no direct connection to the Ministry of Justice. And on top of that you were not the minister of justice yet?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I wasn't. I had only just been appointed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: You are aware that attached to various army corps there were also commissions for exchange of prisoners?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There were municipal commissions and commissions attached to army corps. Municipal commissions had been set up by Crisis Staffs and were later renamed war commissions. That's what I was trying to explain. It was a period when the whole territory held by Serbs was divided into bits and pieces that had no communication amongst themselves. Roads were cut off and telecommunications too.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: On page 9513 of yesterday's transcript, you said that Mr. Colovic resigned at some point?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that. He was given a different position.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Now, I'd like to show you another document from your 92 ter package. It's 65 ter 1401. The date is 14 July 1992. It was sent by the Ministry of Justice and thereby the Ministry of Justice sends to the municipality of Ilidza, in this case, the government decision to appoint Nenad Vanovac, chairman of the central commission, for the exchange of POWs and others?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, somebody signed this for me and informed that this Vanovac was going to replace Colovic as chairman of the commission. He was appointed by the government, and somebody signed this on my behalf.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we see page 2 of this document. I'm being told there's no page 2. I'll come back to this issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Let me show you one more document, 92 ter package 65 ter 1986. This is a contract that the chairman of this commission Nenad Vanovac signed on the 5th of July, 1992, with the chairman of the Federations commission and with the mediation of the UNPROFOR. It's an agreement to release prisoners all for all.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: You know that on the 11th of July, in fact, I hope you know that on the 11th of July an agreement was reached between Dr. Karadzic and Mr. Izetbegovic on the exchange of prisoners.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we see page 2.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is the agreement of 11 July 1992. If we can just see the last page, page 4 in e-court. It's 5 in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Do you see the signature of Radovan Karadzic and --

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nenad Vanovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Nenad Vanovac, chairman of the commission. And this is a copy that, I suppose, was given to the other side, Mr. Izetbegovic and Filip Vukovic, for them to sign?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Court's indulgence. I had given the 65 ter number, and my assistant suggests that it's P1318.26, already an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, let's move on to a different topic you discussed with Ms. Korner. You spoke about prisons and explained the jurisdictions of military and civilian authorities. And you explained that again in response to a question by His Honour Judge Harhoff. We have seen that instruction issued by the minister of defence, and on page 9536, when you were asked to give an explanation about the prison in Vogosca, you said the prison was divided between jurisdictions into one section in the jurisdiction of the army and another section run by the court.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And yesterday you spoke about it on this page that I referred to and you said that in the section run by the court there were only two persons that had been charged.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Persons against whom the court had instituted proceedings because all the people imprisoned during the state of immediate threat of war fell under the jurisdiction of the military authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: We'll come to that. When you gave this answer, you made a comparison which I think is a very good one. You compared the situation in the prison in Vogosca with the situation that prevails in the Scheveningen prison where the entire building is under the jurisdiction of the Dutch Ministry of Justice, however, the UN Detention Unit is a section where totally different rules apply; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: The jurisdiction under the section which constitutes the UN Detention Unit allies only with this Tribunal. It is nothing to do with either the Dutch authorities or Dutch courts; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did that for the benefit of the Trial Chamber so that they can grasp the situation that existed in certain prisons in Republika Srpska. This refers to Vogosca Correctional and Penal Facility, Butmir, and others.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: On page 9540 of yesterday's transcript, we cited another example relating to the current situation of Sarajevo Butmir prison. Let us not repeat that, but the essence, Mr. Mandic, is, and I hope you will agree with me, is that the organ conducting proceedings against certain individual under the law is responsible for this individual and his rights?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this was illustrated by the examples that I cited both in Holland and in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And the same applied to Republika Srpska in 1992, the same principle?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These two examples illustrate the situation in Republika Srpska in 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. A third set of questions that Ms. Korner tackled in examination-in-chief refers to the election and appointment of judges, and reactions of certain MPs to the proposals coming from your ministry relating to the appointment of judges. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: On that occasion you were shown document 65 ter 2722, which is tab 77 in the Prosecution binder.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And can we please look at it again. It's 65 ter 2722.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember that document, sir?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: You saw it yesterday?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I please have page 6 in Serbian. I don't know which page it is in English, but since we are just looking for a specific name, I think it will suffice.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: It was suggested at the time by the Prosecution that crossed out are the candidates in this list were actually stricken out on the grounds of their being non-Serbs. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: You can see here under number 34 --
